extracted.intended_audience: OSHA-regulated employers, chemical manufacturers/importers/distributors, occupational safety and health professionals, OSHA compliance officers, and stakeholders participating in HCS rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for updating and complying with OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard (HCS) as finalized to align with revisions to the UN GHS, including SDS and labeling requirements, legal authority tests, stakeholder engagement, and supporting economic/administrative analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic revision to maintain alignment with the GHS and scientific progress
rubrics_metrics.description: The HCS requires periodic revision to maintain consistency with the GHS and incorporate the progression of scientific principles and best approaches for classification and communication of workplace hazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA updates the HCS to reflect GHS revisions and developments in science, technology, and communication practices; revisions are expected periodically to keep pace with evolving hazard determination processes and improved communication systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: SDS format and Section 9 content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The GHS 16-section SDS format is the standard; updates to SDS content (for example, Section 9) should include additional physical characteristics such as particle characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adoption and retention of the 16-section SDS format improves readability and reduces redundancy; adding particle characteristics in Section 9 is intended to better identify exposure issues (e.g., for nanomaterials) and improve hazard information required for such materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labels and SDSs must be accurate and complete based on all available evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: While the HCS does not require testing of chemicals, it requires that labels and SDSs have accurate information based on all available evidence and that manufacturers, importers, distributors, and employers provide the complete information on the hazards available to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without a complete picture of hazards, downstream users cannot protect themselves. Employers and suppliers must include information needed for workers to know how to adequately protect themselves and safely handle chemicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: SDS content minimums — ingredient identification, hazard classification, precautionary statements, exposure controls, toxicology
rubrics_metrics.description: SDSs should include clear identification of substances/mixtures; correct hazard identification and classification (including carcinogens and sensitizers); appropriate precautionary statements; exposure controls/personal protective equipment; and toxicological information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA cites multiple studies showing frequent SDS deficiencies (missing ingredient info, ambiguous or incorrect classifications, missing safe-handling precautions, missing PPE/exposure control info, and missing toxicological data) and final-rule updates (including Appendix D) aim to remedy these deficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of non-animal and computational test methods for certain hazard classes
rubrics_metrics.description: GHS updates (and corresponding HCS updates) incorporate non-animal test methods (in vitro) and computational/in silico techniques for hazard determination and classification (e.g., skin corrosion/irritation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 3.2 updates and corresponding HCS Appendix A.2 revisions recognize alternative (non-animal) methods as valid for classification; agencies should incorporate these methods where appropriate in hazard determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of behavioral science to improve hazard communication effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques and processes developed in the behavioral sciences should be used to develop more effective communication practices for occupational safety and health purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA references behavioral-science-informed improvements and expects these approaches to inform design and presentation of labels, SDSs, pictograms, and precautionary statements to enhance worker comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate and revise pictograms and precautionary statements based on comprehension studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Precautionary statements and pictograms used in the GHS/HCS should be evaluated for effectiveness and revised based on studies of comprehension and usability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA cites studies that have led to evolution of pictograms/statements; continued evaluation should drive future revisions to improve worker understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonization with international trading partners and federal agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Updates to the HCS should facilitate cooperation with international trading partners (e.g., Canada) and align with other U.S. agencies where appropriate to ease compliance and strengthen worker protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include aligning exemptions for labeling small containers and guidance on using prescribed concentration ranges for trade secrets with Canada's HPR, and coordination with EPA, DOT, and other agencies to avoid conflict and ease international compliance burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bulk shipment labeling flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: For bulk shipments, labels may be placed on the immediate container or transmitted with shipping papers, bills of lading, or by other technological or electronic means, provided full label information is immediately available to workers in printed form on receipt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach recognizes DOT placarding issues for bulk shipments while ensuring downstream users receive full label information upon receipt; intended to increase flexibility without reducing worker protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of DOT pictograms on shipped containers
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a DOT-required pictogram appears on the label for a shipped container, the HCS pictogram for the same hazard may also be provided but is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change acknowledges overlapping regulatory regimes and avoids duplicative pictogram requirements when DOT placarding/pictograms are present on shipped containers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform approach to small-container labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a uniform approach to labeling small containers to ensure critical hazard information is included, addressing issues of limited label space, readability, and special needs for fold-out labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA revised rules to address stakeholder concerns (insufficient space, poor readability, fold-out label challenges) so that critical information appears on labels regardless of container size; see Summary and Explanation for (f)(12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relabeling requirements for chemicals released for shipment (distribution-cycle issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revise relabeling requirements to address difficulty manufacturers face when updating labels as new information becomes available during long distribution cycles, while maintaining worker protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph (f)(11) revisions aim to reduce compliance difficulty for long distribution chains but preserve the requirement that downstream users receive updated hazard information important to worker safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare Final Economic Analysis and Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis Certification
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA must prepare a Final Economic Analysis (FEA), including a Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis Certification, and make supporting materials (e.g., cost-estimate spreadsheets) available in the public docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FEA should include annualized cost estimates (OSHA reported net cost savings of $29.8 million/year at 7% discount and $30.7 million/year at 3% discount) and be accessible (docket OSHA-2019-0001). Economic analyses inform rulemaking and demonstrate benefits/costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update Appendix D to clarify SDS information requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Revisions to Appendix D (based in part on GHS revisions) should clarify the information needed in SDSs—for example, adding particle characteristics and other items necessary to address identified SDS deficiencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix D updates are intended to remedy problems identified in studies (generic/incomplete SDSs, missing info for mixtures and nanomaterials) and to improve the hazard information required for worker protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: OSHA should issue guidance, LOIs, and enforcement directives to clarify HCS provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA will continue to develop guidance documents, issue Letters of Interpretation (LOIs), and publish enforcement directives to assist employers and employees with understanding and complying with the HCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LOIs have clarified issues such as labeling of small containers, labeling of chemicals released for shipment, and use of concentration ranges for trade secrets; OSHA may publish updated directives for compliance officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider stakeholder input in developing regulatory positions and final rules
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA engages stakeholders through meetings, interagency public meetings, public hearings, and docket comments; the Interagency Group and OSHA consider these comments when developing U.S. positions and finalizing rule text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA held public meetings (e.g., 2016, 2018), informal hearings, and received hundreds of submissions; stakeholder suggestions (training modules, leveraging technology, guidance topics) are considered in rulemaking and guidance development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal threshold — Significant risk finding and reliance on prior determinations where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Before promulgating a permanent health or safety standard, OSHA must make a threshold finding that a significant risk is present and that such risk can be eliminated or lessened by a change in practices; where a prior finding exists (e.g., 2012 HCS), OSHA may rely on it for related updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases (e.g., Indus. Union Dep't v. Am. Petroleum Inst.) explain the requirement. OSHA stated it need not make additional findings for this final rule because the HCS previously addressed a significant risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 6(b)(5) feasibility and standard-setting obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 6(b)(5) of the OSH Act, OSHA must set the health standard that 'most adequately assures, to the extent feasible, on the basis of the best available evidence, that no employee will suffer material impairment of health or functional capacity' from workplace exposures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires balancing worker protection goals with feasibility constraints, and treating worker health as paramount unless attainment is unachievable; courts have interpreted Congress's intent to prioritize worker health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and use of 'best available evidence' in rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Best available evidence' includes the latest available scientific data, research, demonstrations, experiments, and experience gained under this and other health and safety laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA must base determinations and standards on such evidence when promulgating or modifying health standards; administrative decisions will be judged against whether they are supported by substantial evidence in the record as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 6(b)(7) labeling/warning mandate and authority to modify
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 6(b)(7) requires standards to prescribe labels or other forms of warning necessary to apprise employees of hazards, relevant symptoms, emergency treatment, and proper precautions, and authorizes modification of these requirements based on experience, information, or new developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision underpins HCS labeling and warning obligations and provides express authority to modify warning requirements as warranted by subsequent experience or technological/medical developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping and rulemaking authority (Sections 8(c) and 8(g)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 8(c)(1) empowers OSHA to require employers to make, keep, and preserve records and make them available; Section 8(g)(2) authorizes the Secretary to prescribe rules/regulations necessary to carry out responsibilities under the OSH Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutory authorities support OSHA's power to require documentation and to issue regulatory changes necessary for implementing standards like the HCS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative procedure requirement — reasoned analysis and substantial-evidence support
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the APA and judicial precedent (e.g., Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm), regulatory agencies may revise rules provided changes are supported by a reasoned analysis and, where applicable, by substantial evidence in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA must explain the basis for rule changes and ensure the rulemaking record supports its determinations; prior administrative findings and the record are relevant to judicial review.
